top_choice_rationale: P001 (Autor, Hanson, Katz) is the best-supported achievement on the common criteria. It pairs a mature framework, the supply-and-demand account of the skill premium and wage structure, with design-based local-labour-market evidence on technology and trade exposure. The core work spans roughly three decades, has been replicated across countries and criticised hard, and the open disputes concern the magnitude and persistence of effects, not their existence. Katz anchors the long-run wage-structure strand that makes the trade evidence a statement about labour demand and not only about local adjustment. The citation can be worded to avoid claiming origination of the task framework and to stay distinct from the 2023 and 2024 prizes. The weak points are Katz's marginal credit given his work with Goldin and Dorn's exclusion by the three-name cap. P002 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) is a defensible, cleaner trade-shock prize and ranks second, but it drops the skill-premium framework. Both rank above no award, because B006 meets the maturity and attribution thresholds well enough to award.
recusal_note: Persson, credited on B007, is at IIES, my home institute. B007 is not in this slate, so the tie does not bear on the ranking. I have long-standing co-authorship with Hassler (chair) and Boppart (co-opted member), both of whom support P001, so their agreement is not independent confirmation of my view. My capital-skill complementarity work is close to the skill-premium strand of B006, which I disclose as field proximity. No tie to Autor, Hanson, Katz or Dorn is apparent from my profile. Disclosed and not adjudicated.
